name: PPE/PS (Modified Polyphenylene Ether)
chemical_makeup: Polyphenylene ether / polystyrene blend (modified PPO, Noryl-type). Neat PPE is effectively unprocessable by melt extrusion, so every commercial grade is alloyed with polystyrene, which drops the melt viscosity into a printable range while diluting the heat resistance. The resulting blend is fully amorphous — the reason it warps far less than the semi-crystalline members of the high-performance group — and, unusually among engineering plastics, it has essentially no ester or amide linkages to hydrolyse, which is the basis of its standout resistance to hot water and steam.
summary: The hydrolysis-proof, low-warp member of the high-performance group. It will sit in boiling water long-term without losing properties, holds tolerance better than anything else printing above 300 °C, and carries UL94 V-0 with a UV F1 rating — at roughly $104/kg, a fraction of the PAEK tier. What it does not offer is strength: 67 MPa tensile puts it in PETG territory, so it is chosen for stability and environment, not for load. Deltas vs pc: better hydrolytic and dimensional behaviour and a V-0 rating, but a 310 °C nozzle and a 120 °C bed that most machines cannot reach, and a much thinner ecosystem.

printing.notes: 290-320 °C nozzle and a 90-120 °C bed put this above every commodity machine and outside a stock Bambu hotend, though within reach of an X1E/H2D-class high-temperature hotend and most well-built enclosed printers with a high-temp bed. A 50-80 °C chamber is recommended and helps first layers on large footprints, but heated_chamber_required is false — being amorphous, PPE/PS does not carry the crystallisation-driven shrinkage that makes chamber heat mandatory for peek or pc-pbt. Part cooling off or very low. Unfilled, so a stock nozzle is fine. Filamentcheatsheet lists 195-220 °C for what appears to be the same product; that figure is roughly 100 °C below the manufacturer TDS and is treated as an aggregation error (see conflicts).

feeding.notes: Rigid, unfilled and non-abrasive, so nothing in the feed path objects mechanically, but direct drive is preferred at these extrusion pressures. AMS is 'no' on process temperature alone: 290-320 °C is outside what any consumer material station feeds, and no vendor documents PPE/PS in one (unverified).

drying.dryness_validation: Clear glossy extrudate with no popping at the nozzle. PPE/PS rarely fails this check — unlike the nylons, a sealed spool is normally print-ready without a cycle.
drying.notes: 3DXTech specifies 80 °C for 4 h, and 'if-exposed' rather than 'always' is the honest setting: the blend has no hydrolysable linkages, so it neither absorbs much water nor degrades from the water it does absorb. This is the same property that lets finished parts live in boiling water, and it makes PPE/PS one of the least moisture-fussy materials printing above 300 °C.

storage.recommendations: Ordinary sealed storage with desiccant. No drybox discipline is needed and a lapse is recoverable with a short 80 °C cycle.

price.notes: Approximately $104/kg from the 3DXTech ThermaX PPE/PS listing — a single-vendor datapoint, so the broader market band is unverified. That is roughly double pc and a quarter to a tenth of the PAEK tier, which is the value proposition: high-performance behaviour on several axes at an engineering-plastic price.

recommended: dimensionally stable precision parts and tooling
parts exposed to hot water, steam or repeated wet-heat cycling
UL94 V-0 rated enclosures and electrical housings
low-warp jigs and fixtures at large footprints
outdoor housings needing a UV F1 rating
plumbing and fluid-handling fixtures where hydrolysis kills polyesters
not_recommended: high-strength structural parts — 67 MPa is PETG-class
budget printers and stock hotends (290-320 °C and a 120 °C bed)
chemically aggressive service — the polystyrene phase is attacked by many solvents
cost-sensitive work where pc would do

properties.notes: HDT 112 °C is quoted at 1.8 MPa — the harsher of the two standard loads, so it is not directly comparable with the 0.45 MPa figures given elsewhere in this catalog and understates the material relative to them. Marketing copy for the same product cites 120 °C without stating a load (see conflicts). Tg 128 °C. Tensile 67 MPa, which is the honest weak point: strong for a commodity plastic, unremarkable for something printing at 310 °C. Density 1.10 g/cm³, among the lightest materials in the high-performance group. UL94 V-0 flame rating and a UL746C F1 outdoor-weathering rating — the combination of V-0 and F1 is rare in this catalog. Hydrolytic stability is the headline: the blend withstands long-term immersion in boiling water without property loss, which no polyester or polyamide here will do. Shrinkage is not published and is left blank, but being amorphous it is low.

compatibility.notes: No bonding or support pairings are documented for PPE/PS in the sources reviewed and none are asserted. The polystyrene phase suggests a styrenic affinity in principle, but nothing in the ABS/ASA/HIPS group survives contact with a 290-320 °C melt, so a hips breakaway interface — the obvious guess — is not viable and is deliberately omitted. pva and bvoh degrade roughly 100 °C below the print window. Same-material breakaway support is the practical route; that is slicer behaviour rather than an interface pairing and is not recorded here (RESEARCH_GUIDE §8).

alternatives.reason: Cheaper, far more widely stocked and printable on ordinary enclosed hardware at 250-280 °C rather than 310 °C — with a higher heat score (9 vs 8) and much better strength — but PC hydrolyses in hot water and steam where PPE/PS does not (water 7 vs 10), and it carries no V-0 rating.

A much higher ceiling (continuous service ~180 °C against ~110 °C) with comparable amorphous dimensional stability and its own V-0 rating — at roughly twice to three times the price, a 150 °C drying specification and a nozzle beyond any consumer hotend.

When the part is actually loaded: 105 MPa in-plane against 67 MPa and an HDT of 180 °C @1.8 MPa against 112 °C — giving up the V-0 rating, the hydrolytic stability, the low warp (5 vs 4) and adding a 120 °C drying cycle and a hardened nozzle.

emissions.notes: The polystyrene phase means styrene is a plausible emission, as it is for the styrenics, and the 290-320 °C process temperature is far above the range where that becomes significant — particulate emission scales steeply with nozzle temperature and this is near the top of what a non-industrial machine reaches. Ventilation is recorded 'required' on that combination. No PPE/PS-specific emissions measurement was found (unverified); the styrene attribution is inferred from the blend chemistry rather than measured. Vent externally or filter through HEPA plus activated carbon, and let the enclosure clear before opening.

safety_notes: A 310 °C hotend and a 120 °C bed inside a warm enclosure are serious burn hazards, and the enclosure concentrates styrene-bearing off-gas — let it clear before opening. The V-0 rating describes the finished part's flame behaviour and says nothing about the safety of the printing process. Not food-contact suitable as printed, despite the hot-water tolerance: hydrolytic stability is not the same as food certification, and no certified line was found.
additional_notes: PPE/PS is a specification material rather than a general-purpose one. Pick it when the failure mode you are designing against is hot water, steam, warp on a large flat part, or a flame test — it beats everything cheaper on those four axes simultaneously. Do not pick it for strength, and do not pick it for chemical resistance in general: the polystyrene phase is attacked by solvents that PPE alone would shrug off, which is the standing trade-off of every Noryl-type blend. Tectonic's ATAR FST1 grade is marketed on fire/smoke/toxicity performance for transport applications; its specific FST ratings were not verified in this pass.

provenance.conflicts: Two disagreements, one of them severe. Nozzle temperature: filamentcheatsheet lists 195-220 °C for what appears to be the same product, against the 3DXTech TDS's 290-320 °C — roughly 100 °C apart. The TDS is treated as authoritative and the aggregator figure is recorded here as an apparent error rather than a competing formulation; 195-220 °C is not a plausible melt range for any PPE blend. HDT: the TDS gives 112 °C at 1.8 MPa while the product's marketing copy cites 120 °C with no load stated; 112 °C at the specified load is recorded and the marketing figure is flagged. Price rests on a single vendor listing. Emissions are inferred from blend chemistry and process temperature with no PPE/PS-specific measurement found. Shrinkage, print speed and any bonding or support pairings are undocumented in the sources reviewed. The Tectonic ATAR FST1 grade's fire/smoke/toxicity ratings were not verified.

trade_names.notes: The source of this entry's recorded figures: 290-320 °C nozzle, 90-120 °C bed, HDT 112 °C @1.8 MPa, UL94 V-0.
Marketed on fire/smoke/toxicity performance for transport applications; specific FST ratings not verified in this pass.
